haiku-low.q1: MySQL first: commit the user change with its outbox row, then one inline Postgres copy with a 200 ms timeout. A Postgres failure is logged and counted; the caller still sees success.
haiku-low.q2: Only when the existing Postgres row's version is lower than the incoming version, and no Postgres tombstone exists for that id. Otherwise the copy does nothing.
haiku-low.q3: Step 4 dual writes must be on everywhere for at least 60 s, with outbox age under 5 min. The flag cache lasts 30 s, so instances can disagree that long.
haiku-low.q4: One runner copies 2,000 rows per batch in id order. It checks replica lag before each batch and waits, polling every 5 s, while lag is above 5 s.
haiku-low.q5: Reads move only after a full compare pass is clean with zero mismatches. The source of truth moves only after 72 h at 100% reads, a clean compare, and other stated checks.
haiku-low.q6: The forward outbox row in MySQL users_pg_outbox records it. The forward worker copies the current MySQL row to Postgres every 1 s, then deletes the outbox row.
haiku-low.q7: Erasure writes the Postgres tombstone first, under the per-user lock. Every copy takes that lock, checks the tombstone, and skips the copy if one exists.
haiku-low.q8: Progress is backfill_last_id in Postgres migration_state, committed in the same transaction as each batch. The runner stops when a batch returns 0 rows, or when its lease token no longer matches.
haiku-low.q9: The full compare and repair pass (step 6) hashes 2,000-id chunks. Differing rows are deferred if the MySQL outbox holds them; otherwise the copy rules repair Postgres and count a mismatch.
haiku-low.q10: Instances poll only the store that holds the source of truth, and a new mode is written there first, so none applies pg early. Past 60 s the switch resumes MySQL; by 75 s it aborts.
haiku-low.q11: Postgres assigns ids after the switch, from the MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT plus 1,000,000. MySQL assigns none, and after rollback its AUTO_INCREMENT is set to max(id)+1.
haiku-low.q12: The reverse outbox worker copies changes to MySQL, and erasures are mirrored there. Rollback pauses in Postgres, drains the outbox, verifies rows, then switches mode. It ends at pg_only, no sooner than 14 days after the switch.

sonnet.q1: Commit to MySQL first (together with a forward outbox row in the same transaction), then one inline Postgres copy is tried with a 200 ms timeout. If the Postgres part fails or times out, it is logged and counted but never raised; the caller's request still succeeds.
sonnet.q2: Only when the existing row's version is lower than the incoming copy's version (the version rule). If the id is missing it inserts; otherwise (equal or higher existing version) it does nothing. Also skipped if a tombstone exists for the id.
sonnet.q3: Step 4 (dual writes) must have been on everywhere for at least 60 s (every instance reporting app_flag_value users.dual_write on, then wait 60 s), and outbox age must be under 5 min (steps 2 and 3 live on every instance). Instances can disagree for up to 30 s after a flag change (30 s flag cache).
sonnet.q4: It reads from the replica (not the primary), in batches of 2000 ids by primary-key order, and before each batch checks mysql_replica_lag_seconds; if lag is above 5 s it waits and rechecks every 5 s. A single runner holds a lease. (Reporting jobs also use the replica.)
sonnet.q5: Reads: backfill complete and a full compare/repair pass clean (zero mismatches, no deferred row still differing); then ramp 1/10/50/100% with no counted sampled mismatches. Source of truth: reads at 100% for at least 72 h, a clean full compare started after the latest clock start, outbox age under 5 min and depth small, every instance on the fenced build, and the reverse worker deployed on every instance and passing its checks.
sonnet.q6: The forward outbox row (users_pg_outbox in MySQL), written in the same MySQL transaction as the user write, records that the Postgres copy may be stale. The forward worker (every 1 s on every instance) re-reads the current MySQL row, copies it to Postgres with the copy rules, and deletes the outbox rows only after the copy succeeds, retrying until it does.
sonnet.q7: Tombstones: every copy takes the per-user lock, checks the tombstone in the target store and skips if one exists. Erasure inserts the Postgres tombstone (and deletes the Postgres row) first under the lock, then the MySQL tombstone/delete. A copy that read the row before deletion finds the tombstone and skips; so does a later one. Tombstones are never deleted.
sonnet.q8: In Postgres migration_state.backfill_last_id (the highest id in the last committed batch, starting at 0), updated in the same Postgres transaction as the batch's rows, so it matches what was copied. The runner holds a lease with owner token (60 s expiry) and the checkpoint update only applies if the token matches. It stops when a batch returns 0 rows (about 19,000 batches).
sonnet.q9: The full comparison and repair job (step 6): it hashes (id, version, email, name, plan, updated_at) per chunk of 2,000 ids, skipping tombstoned ids. For differing rows, under the per-user lock it re-reads both; if the user still has forward outbox rows the row is deferred (rechecked at the end of the pass); otherwise if still different, the copy rules repair Postgres and it counts as a mismatch. A pass is clean with zero mismatches and no deferred row still differing.
sonnet.q10: Via the control row with mode and epoch and the write fence/lease: writes MySQL paused (epoch+1), wait 12 s so all in-flight writes end (leases/3 s deadlines guarantee this), drain the forward outbox, then write pg (epoch+2) to Postgres and then to MySQL; instances poll MySQL so they stay paused until they see pg, then all apply it within about 2 s. If it runs long: if still draining at 60 s (before step 4 writes), write mysql (epoch+3) and resume; if pg in Postgres but not MySQL, retry the MySQL write, and if not done by 75 s abort by writing mysql (epoch+3) to MySQL then Postgres. Total pause at most 90 s (target about 30 s). If MySQL has pg and some instances applied it, do not flip back plainly; use the step 11 rollback.
sonnet.q11: Postgres assigns ids from its sequence, which is set at the switch to MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT plus 1,000,000; MySQL assigns no new ids after the switch (reverse copies insert explicit ids). On rollback, MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT is set to max(id)+1 so it cannot assign an id Postgres already used.
sonnet.q12: The reverse outbox (pg_outbox) in Postgres: each Postgres write adds a row in the same commit, and the reverse worker copies changes to MySQL under the MySQL per-user lock with tombstone check and version rule. Rollback (step 11): write paused to Postgres and wait 12 s, drain the reverse outbox to zero and verify every Postgres row/tombstone has a MySQL match, copy the erasure work list to MySQL and set AUTO_INCREMENT to max(id)+1, then write mode mysql to MySQL then Postgres (at most 90 s, abort at 75 s). The option ends at step 12 (pg_only, no sooner than 14 days after source_switched_at); rollback is impossible after that.
